authoredPrompt: This figure shows a single planar point set with its convex hull traced as a thick gray polygon. Five hull vertices appear as filled black dots and are labeled p_0 at the bottom left, p_1 at the lower right, p_2 at the right, p_3 at the top, and p_4 at the left; eight further black dots lie scattered inside the polygon, joined to nothing. A dashed straight line passes through p_0 and continues upward through p_3; at both of those vertices a pair of short arrows straddles the dashed line, reading left chain with an arrow pointing left and right chain with an arrow pointing right. Every hull vertex also carries a short vertical tick and a horizontal reference ray: at p_0, p_1, and p_2 the ray points right, and a thin arc sweeps from it around to the next hull edge, the arc at p_0 being very narrow and the one at p_2 close to a half turn. At p_4 and p_3 the ray points left instead, with arcs swept from it the same way. The arcs are the quantities being compared, since the next vertex along the boundary is the one subtending the smallest such angle. The picture lays out the wrapping order in which hull vertices are discovered, first up the right chain to the highest point and then back down the left.
authoredInteractions:
- Button for stepping through Jarvis's march from p0 to p4: the active reference ray, angle sweep, and next hull edge light up at each vertex, making clear how the smallest polar angle chooses the next boundary point.
- Toggle between right-chain and left-chain construction: the horizontal reference direction flips at the highest and lowest points and the active half of the hull is emphasized, making clear why the wrapping rule changes direction across the two chains.
- Hover for any interior point during a step: its candidate angle appears beside the chosen hull angle, making clear why interior points are skipped even though they are in the same point set.
authoredContext:
Jarvis’s march computes the convex hull of a set Q of points by a technique known as package wrapping (or gift wrapping). The algorithm runs in time O.nh/, where h is the number of vertices of CH.Q/. When h is o.lg n/, Jarvis’s march is asymptotically faster than Graham’s scan. Intuitively, Jarvis’s march simulates wrapping a taut piece of paper around the set Q. We start by taping the end of the paper to the lowest point in the set, that is, to the same point p0 with which we start Graham’s scan. We know that this point must be a vertex of the convex hull. We pull the paper to the right to make it taut, and then we pull it higher until it touches a point. This point must also be a vertex of the convex hull. Keeping the paper taut, we continue in this way around the set of vertices until we come back to our original point p0. More formally, Jarvis’s march builds a sequence H D hp0; p1; : : : ; ph1i of the vertices of CH.Q/. We start with p0. As Figure 33.9 shows, the next vertex p1 in the convex hull has the smallest polar angle with respect to p0. (In case of ties, we choose the point farthest from p0.) Similarly, p2 has the smallest polar angle with respect to p1, and so on. When we reach the highest vertex, say pk (breaking
ties by choosing the farthest such vertex), we have constructed, as Figure 33.9
shows, the right chain of CH.Q/. To construct the left chain, we start at pk and
choose pkC1 as the point with the smallest polar angle with respect to pk, but from
the negative x-axis. We continue on, forming the left chain by taking polar angles
from the negative x-axis, until we come back to our original vertex p0.
We could implement Jarvis’s march in one conceptual sweep around the convex
hull, that is, without separately constructing the right and left chains. Such implementations typically keep track of the angle of the last convex-hull side chosen and
require the sequence of angles of hull sides to be strictly increasing (in the range
of 0 to 2_x0019_ radians). The advantage of constructing separate chains is that we need
not explicitly compute angles; the techniques of Section 33.1 suffice to compare
angles.
If implemented properly, Jarvis’s march has a running time of O.nh/. For each
of the h vertices of CH.Q/, we find the vertex with the minimum polar angle. Each
comparison between polar angles takes O.1/ time, using the techniques of Section 33.1. As Section 9.1 shows, we can compute the minimum of n values in O.n/
time if each comparison takes O.1/ time. Thus, Jarvis’s march takes O.nh/ time.

discrepancies: The default generated figure adds an orange highlighted hull edge, an orange sweep arrow, a translucent blue chain highlight, and a 'chosen θ = 7°' annotation that are not present in the monochrome source figure.
The source is entirely black/gray, while the generated default state introduces blue/orange interactive emphasis colors, changing the visual character of the diagram.
The generated figure is scaled down substantially within the canvas, making labels and interior points much smaller relative to the available space than in the source.
The bottom 'left chain'/'right chain' labels and arrows are more cramped around p0 and the lower edge than in the source, and the added active-angle label overlaps the lower hull edge area.
Some reference rays and sweep arcs differ slightly in length and placement from the source, especially around p0 and p3, though the overall topology is preserved.
evaluation.notes: The hull topology, point labels, dashed divider, chain labels, and sweep arcs are recognizable, but the default colored Jarvis-step overlay and extra angle annotation prevent it from matching the static source as a drop-in replacement.
action_items: Make the initial/default state match the source exactly: remove or hide the orange active edge, active sweep arrow, translucent chain highlight, and 'chosen θ' label until the user starts the interactive demo.
Use the source's monochrome styling by default, reserving blue/orange/green highlights only for explicitly activated interaction states.
Increase the drawing scale or reduce excess whitespace so the figure fills the available canvas more like the source and labels are comfortably readable.
Reposition the bottom chain labels/arrows and any interactive angle label so they do not crowd p0 or overlap the lower hull edge.
